actions.reason: RegexTokenizer.encode_ordinary and BasicTokenizer.encode re-derived the ordered merge list on every call. Each call sorted merges with a Python key function, validated all entries in a Python loop, and rebuilt every pair string with chr(). encode() with special tokens calls encode_ordinary once per text part, so that work was repeated many times. A new helper, base.ordered_merge_steps, computes the validated index-ordered list of (pair str, idx char, idx) once. It caches the list for the last merges dict, and only valid results are cached. A cache hit requires the same dict object, contents equal to a stored copy, and int-only key elements and values, so a mutated or int-subclass merge table is re-validated. The regex path keeps its extra conditions: first id > 255 and last id < 0x10ffff, which the strictly increasing ids make equivalent to the old per-entry check. Separator choice and fallback paths are unchanged. Equivalence harness outputs are identical; encode_ir ratio 0.9812.

journal.text:
I changed how encode gets its merge order. RegexTokenizer.encode_ordinary and BasicTokenizer.encode rebuilt the ordered merge list on every call. Each call sorted merges with a Python key function, validated every entry in a loop, and rebuilt pair strings with chr(). I added base.ordered_merge_steps in minbpe/base.py and pointed both encode paths at it. The basic.py and regex.py encode bodies got shorter.

Sandbox evaluation, 66 changed lines, outputs identical. encode_ir went from 739481361 to 725600894, ratio 0.9812. The other metrics rose slightly: train_basic_ir 1.0006, train_regex_ir 1.0007, decode_ir 1.0030, save_load_ir 1.0011. All guards were within limits. It is submitted and waiting on replays.

I believe per-call setup was a real cost in encode, mainly when special tokens split text into many parts. The gain is small. The decode_ir rise is unexplained, since I did not touch decode.

Next, check why decode_ir moved. Then profile the inner merge loop in encode, which is likely the larger cost.
